abstract: ArXiv:2611.10827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the quantum-channel optimization of Alrabiah and Guruswami to [MATH]-ary constant-composition codes. We study explicit channel and flag constructions that recover selected classical asymptotic upper bounds, including the Ben-Haim--Litsyn, moving-subspace and Horn-channel bounds. We give two equivalent formulations, Gram and flag, and prove stability of the obtained upper bounds under permutation transport and generalized shortening. A hierarchy defined by bounding the output-state ranks within each flag improves strictly between consecutive levels at every composition and every positive distance below the Plotkin threshold. We provide finite matrix parametrizations of these bounds (i.e., the number of variables does not depend on the length of codes under consideration). Numerical optimization rapidly produces improvements over the known asymptotic upper bounds throughout all tested nonbinary parameter ranges. For rational input data, each finite level admits near-optimal feasible rational descriptions of polynomial length. Their feasibility can be checked exactly and their objective values computed to any prescribed accuracy in polynomial time; the associated threshold problem with a prescribed gap belongs to [MATH].
tldr: The paper develops quantum-channel-inspired optimization bounds for q-ary constant-composition codes and improves several classical asymptotic upper bounds.
motivation: It aims to extend the Alrabiah-Guruswami quantum-channel optimization framework to constant-composition codes and recover or improve known classical coding bounds.
method: The authors introduce equivalent Gram and flag formulations, finite matrix parametrizations, and a rank-based hierarchy of bounds that is stable under permutation transport and generalized shortening.
result: The hierarchy strictly improves between levels and numerical optimization yields improved asymptotic upper bounds for nonbinary parameter ranges, with rational feasibility checks of polynomial length.
conclusion: The work is a technically deep contribution to coding theory and channel-based optimization, but it is only tangentially connected to the core quantum information interests of entanglement, cryptography, entropy, and quantum channel capacities.

title: Trainability-Simulability Tradeoff In Parameterized IQP-based Reinforcement Learning Policies
authors: Andr\'e Sequeira
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameterized instantaneous quantum polynomial-time (IQP) circuits generate distributions conjectured to be hard to sample classically. As reinforcement learning (RL) policies, their [MATH] measurement outcomes are typically mapped to a smaller action space by a classical decoder. This aggregation can mitigate initialization concentration while making the policy classically simulable. We characterize this tradeoff through the decoder's Fourier--Pauli expansion. Under independent uniform initialization, we express policy variance as an exact sum over groups of nonconstant Pauli components with identical active-generator signatures. Each group contributes its squared aggregate coefficient times [MATH], where [MATH] is the binary rank of its active generators. An inverse-polynomial aggregate coefficient with logarithmic rank prevents exponential policy concentration. Sparse Pauli expansions and contiguous action bins permit efficient classical additive estimation of action probabilities. We introduce a majority decoder combining protected low-weight components with exponentially large exact Fourier support, preserving initialization nonconcentration while excluding polynomial-size enumeration of the exact expansion. Numerical experiments corroborate the variance laws. In ten-qubit CartPole experiments, majority achieves higher returns than recursive parity and the tested local readouts, while higher-weight Pauli sectors contribute an increasing relative share of gradient magnitude during training. A complementary 21-qubit block-chain policy outperforms an extensive pool of fully connected classical neural networks in episode efficiency, even though its bounded-width structure permits efficient classical simulation. These results guide decoder design for quantum and quantum-inspired RL, distinguishing policy nonconcentration, learning performance, and classical simulability.
tldr: The paper analyzes a tradeoff between trainability and classical simulability in parameterized IQP circuits used as reinforcement learning policies, characterized via a Fourier-Pauli expansion and decoder design.
motivation: Parameterized IQP circuits are conjectured to be classically hard to sample, but decoding their measurement outcomes into actions may make them simulable; the work aims to understand and navigate this tradeoff for quantum reinforcement learning.
method: The authors express policy variance under independent uniform initialization as a sum over groups of nonconstant Pauli components, introduce a majority decoder, and test IQP-based policies on CartPole and a 21-qubit block-chain task against classical neural networks.
result: The majority decoder preserves initialization nonconcentration while excluding polynomial-size enumeration of the exact Fourier expansion; it achieves higher CartPole returns than recursive parity and local readouts, and the block-chain policy outperforms many classical networks despite efficient classical simulability.
conclusion: The results provide design principles for decoders in quantum and quantum-inspired reinforcement learning, separating policy nonconcentration, learning performance, and classical simulability.

title: On The Estimation Of Linear-optical Amplitudes And Probabilities With Entangled Input State
authors: Pierre-Emmanuel Emeriau Jean Senellart
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most proposed applications of boson samplers, including photonic machine-learning models, do not use the samples themselves but estimates of output probabilities, marginals or overlaps, obtained to additive precision from a finite number of shots. For product inputs such as single photons, these quantities can already be estimated classically with Gurvits's algorithm and its generalisations. We ask whether entangled inputs change this picture. For any [MATH]-photon input that is a matrix-product state of bond dimension [MATH], with one photon per site and [MATH] modes per site, we give an unbiased estimator of any output amplitude of an [MATH]-mode interferometer, whose mean-square error after [MATH] draws is at most [MATH] whatever the interferometer, the output pattern and the entanglement of the state. Each draw costs [MATH] operations after [MATH] preprocessing, and an additive error [MATH] with probability at least [MATH] requires [MATH] draws, with memory of the order of the input size. The main application is to light emitted sequentially by quantum emitters, such as spin-based sources of photonic cluster states, for which [MATH] is bounded by the dimension of the source's retained quantum memory: one spin gives [MATH] at any length, and a memory of [MATH] qubits, held in emitters or in photons stored in a delay line, gives [MATH], so the cost stays polynomial as long as [MATH]. The same sampler also estimates traced-memory probabilities, overlaps and individual marginal probabilities. All guarantees are additive: the estimator gives neither relative estimates of exponentially small probabilities nor a sampler of the output distribution.
tldr: The paper gives an unbiased classical estimator for output amplitudes and probabilities of linear-optical interferometers with entangled matrix-product-state inputs, with additive-error guarantees.
motivation: Boson-sampler applications often rely on estimating output probabilities, marginals, or overlaps rather than sampling; for product inputs these can be estimated classically, so the authors ask whether entangled inputs change this picture.
method: For an M-photon input represented as a matrix-product state with bond dimension D and one photon per site, they construct an unbiased estimator of any interferometer output amplitude using preprocessing and per-draw operations polynomial in the input size.
result: They bound the mean-square error after N draws uniformly over interferometers and output patterns, and apply the estimator to sequentially emitted photonic cluster states where D is controlled by the emitter memory size.
conclusion: Entangled inputs with bounded matrix-product-state bond dimension still allow efficient additive estimation of amplitudes and certain probabilities, but the guarantees do not provide relative estimates of exponentially small probabilities or a sampler of the output distribution.

title: Beyond The Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle Qaoa Retains On A Superconducting Processor
authors: Mohammad Arif Hossain Sanim Yousuf Fahim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor , with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.
tldr: An experimental benchmarking study of transferred-angle QAOA on IBM's Heron superconducting processor showing that mean-gap metrics overstate what noise actually preserves about the optimal bitstring.
motivation: Hardware QAOA runs are usually validated by comparing mean cost to simulation, but under global depolarization all bitstring probabilities should degrade by the same fraction, so mean-gap agreement may hide severe loss of the optimum itself.
method: Depth-2 transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition were executed at 12 qubits on IBM Heron, with and without dynamical decoupling and Pauli twirling, comparing mean normalized gap, floor-corrected optimum probability, near-optimal set retention, and a device-matched noise model.
result: Main-family circuits retained 29-46% of mean-gap improvement but only 5-15% of the optimum probability, with near-optimal strings lost comparably to the optimum while avoidance of poor strings was retained best; the noise model overestimated optimum retention five- to eightfold, and on a rugged planted family the device found the optimum in 62% of 768-shot blocks versus 98% noiseless.
conclusion: Validation of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and near-optimal sets, not just mean cost, since mean-gap metrics can substantially overstate practically useful QAOA performance on noisy superconducting hardware.

title: A Grover-Amplified Oracle For Maximum Clique On Graph, Minimum Hitting Set And Dualizations On Hypergraphs Built On Quantum Phase Estimation
authors: Francisco Pi\~nero, Fernando L. \pelayo, Hernan I. de la Cruz, Jose J. Paulet, Mauro Mezzini, Fernando Cuartero
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we use a quantum circuit called the Graph Encoding Operator which, applied to the complement [MATH] of any graph [MATH], yields an oracle for the maximum clique problem suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Analogously, we devise a Hypergraph Encoding Operator which, when applied to a hypergraph [MATH], yields an oracle for the minimum hitting set suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Interestingly, the latter oracle provides, when measured, an approximation of the number of hitting sets of the hypergraph, thus solving the dualization problem for positive Boolean functions represented in a positive irredundant disjunctive normal form. We give the full construction of both operators, prove their correctness, analyze their complexity, and provide an implementation on a quantum simulator. We discuss the resulting complexity, contrast them with existing quantum computer algorithms based on Grover search and we will show that our algorithms outperform, to the best of our knowledge, all of the previous algorithms on space computational complexity by requiring only [MATH] number of qubits with respect to the number of vertices [MATH], for representing both graphs and hypergraphs in the encoding operator and, consequently, results in an oracle for both graphs and hypergraphs that uses only [MATH] qubits even when the hypergraph contains an exponential (on the number of vertices) number of hyperedges.
tldr: The paper constructs Grover-amplified oracles for maximum clique and minimum hitting set using graph/hypergraph encoding operators based on quantum phase estimation.
motivation: The authors aim to design space-efficient quantum oracles for combinatorial graph and hypergraph problems and exploit Grover amplification for speedup.
method: They define Graph Encoding and Hypergraph Encoding Operators, prove their correctness, analyze complexity, and simulate implementations on a quantum simulator.
result: The proposed oracles require only a linear number of qubits in the number of vertices, even for hypergraphs with exponentially many hyperedges, and are claimed to outperform prior Grover-based algorithms in space complexity.
conclusion: The work provides a quantum algorithm for maximum clique, minimum hitting set, and dualization with improved qubit-space requirements, but it is a quantum algorithms/complexity contribution rather than a core topic in the researcher's interests.

title: On Relative Greedy Weights
authors: Olav Geil
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Relative greedy weights were introduced by Li and Liu in [19] as a measure of information leakage in coordinated two-party wire-tap channels of type II when the adversary follows a greedy strategy. Their definition can be viewed as a relative version of the CEZ greedy weights, which are only locally greedy. In this paper, we revisit the concept of greediness and relative greediness introducing new measures, and we discuss other perhaps more relevant applications of relative greedy weights than the coordinated two-party wire-tap channel of type II. We pay special attention to bottom-up greedy weights, which correspond to an adversary with an ultimate greedy approach, and we present families of nested codes for which such weights are larger than the relative CEZ greedy weights.
tldr: This paper revisits relative greedy weights in coding theory, introducing new greedy-weight measures and applications to information leakage in coordinated two-party wire-tap channels.
motivation: Relative greedy weights were introduced as a measure of information leakage in coordinated two-party wire-tap channels of type II under a greedy adversary strategy, and the paper aims to clarify and extend this concept.
method: The author revisits greediness and relative greediness, introduces new measures including bottom-up greedy weights, and constructs families of nested codes for comparison.
result: Families of nested codes are presented for which bottom-up greedy weights are larger than relative CEZ greedy weights.
conclusion: Relative greedy weights may have broader relevance beyond the coordinated two-party wire-tap channel of type II, especially for adversaries using an ultimate greedy approach.

title: Efficient SC-Flip Decoding For Polar Codes Through Decision-Boundary Normalization
authors: Gulinisha Yiming, Zhongjun Yang, Zhicheng Liu, Zhiming Ma, Xumin Ni, Yuting Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate first erroneous position (FEP) identification is key to improving the error-correction performance of successive cancellation flip (SCF) decoding. However, FEP identification remains challenging with a limited number of re-decoding attempts. To address this issue, we propose decision-boundary normalization (DBN) to improve FEP identification and develop a novel DBN-SCF decoding algorithm. DBN normalizes the magnitude of each decision log-likelihood ratio (LLR) by the standard deviation predicted by the Gaussian approximation (GA) for the corresponding bit-channel. This allows a single normalized threshold to be shared across bit-channels within each code configuration, giving it a consistent statistical meaning and avoiding per-channel calibration. DBN-SCF decoding selects candidate flip positions from the information set in the natural successive cancellation (SC) decoding order using a threshold, without sorting. Moreover, DBN-SCF decoding achieves better error-correction performance with a limited number of re-decoding attempts. It also requires lower average decoding complexity than existing SCF decoding methods at a comparable level of error-correction performance.
tldr: The paper proposes decision-boundary normalization to improve first erroneous position identification in SC-Flip decoding of polar codes.
motivation: Accurate first erroneous position identification is critical for SC-Flip decoding, but remains difficult when only a limited number of re-decoding attempts are allowed.
method: Decision-boundary normalization normalizes each decision LLR by the Gaussian-approximation-predicted standard deviation for its bit-channel, enabling a shared normalized threshold and threshold-based candidate selection without sorting.
result: DBN-SCF decoding improves error-correction performance with limited re-decoding attempts and achieves lower average decoding complexity than existing SCF methods at comparable performance.
conclusion: The proposed DBN-SCF algorithm offers an efficient approach to classical polar-code decoding but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Practical Ellipse Fitting For Atom Interferometry
authors: N. Fowler, D. B. Reinhardt, M Meister, C. A. Sackett
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In differential atom interferometry, it is necessary to extract the differential phase shift between two interferometers that are individually noisy. A variety of techniques can be used for this purpose, under the general label of ellipse fitting. We compare several methods for ellipse fitting, considering parameters and performance relevant to atom interferometry. Statistical, algebraic, geometric and Bayesian methods are discussed, and we describe a novel "reciprocal" geometric method that offers some benefits. Each method has advantages and disadvantages that depend on the use case required. Supplemental material includes basic Python and Matlab code for each method.
tldr: A comparative study of ellipse-fitting algorithms for extracting differential phase shifts in noisy differential atom interferometry.
motivation: Differential atom interferometry requires robust extraction of a small differential phase between two individually noisy interferometers, where naive fitting methods can introduce bias or excess noise.
method: The authors benchmark statistical, algebraic, geometric, and Bayesian ellipse-fitting techniques on parameters relevant to atom interferometry, and introduce a new 'reciprocal' geometric method; Python and Matlab reference implementations are provided.
result: Each method shows distinct trade-offs in accuracy, bias, and computational cost depending on noise level and use case, with the novel reciprocal geometric approach offering particular advantages in some regimes.
conclusion: No single ellipse-fitting method is universally optimal; the choice should be guided by the specific noise characteristics and precision requirements of the interferometric experiment.

title: Initialization Masks Overcome Decoding Obstructions In Compressed Qaoa
authors: Steven Frankel Emilio Semre
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In compressed quantum optimization, a variational state is converted into a classical assignment by decoding noncommuting observables. We show that this step creates structural restrictions that changing the initialization can remove, even when increasing circuit depth cannot. For an explicit infinite family of connected cubic graphs on [MATH] vertices, with a fixed Pauli encoding and deterministic sign decoder, every all-plus QAOA circuit has cut at most [MATH], at every finite depth and every real angle sequence. A uniform signed product-state mask at fixed depth-one angles has expected cut [MATH], an additive advantage [MATH]; an infinite subfamily admits an optimal mask. A second construction retains a linear depth-one separation under weak weighted couplings, a bounded cost-angle domain and a specified production-encoder ordering. Noiseless simulations then test classical mask selection before energy optimization. On 1,699 random cubic MaxCut instances, one selected mask achieves mean ratio [MATH], versus [MATH] for the all-plus [MATH] baseline and [MATH] for the best of [MATH] separately optimized random masks. On complete cohorts of weighted MaxCut, sparse Ising, Max-2-XOR and Max-2-SAT, the selected mask also improves on the baseline at every size, but it trails the pool at small sizes and leads it significantly only at the larger MaxCut and Ising sizes. Finite-pool order statistics separate the effect of selection from that of drawing a random mask. The results distinguish decoded expressivity from optimized energy and empirical performance; they do not establish a quantum computational advantage.
tldr: The paper shows that decoding noncommuting observables in compressed QAOA creates structural cut-size obstructions that can be removed by using signed product-state initialization masks rather than increasing circuit depth.
motivation: In compressed quantum optimization, converting the variational state into a classical assignment via a sign decoder may impose expressivity limits that are not visible in the optimized energy; the authors ask whether initialization, not depth, can overcome these limits.
method: They construct an infinite family of connected cubic graphs with fixed Pauli encoding and deterministic sign decoder, proving depth-independent cut bounds for all-plus QAOA, then propose uniform signed product-state masks at fixed depth-one angles and test classical mask selection on 1,699 random cubic MaxCut instances and other cohorts.
result: All-plus QAOA circuits achieve at most a capped cut at every finite depth, while a selected mask obtains an additive advantage with provably optimal masks for an infinite subfamily; empirically one selected mask reaches a strong mean ratio, outperforming the all-plus baseline and often approaching or exceeding separately optimized random masks at larger sizes.
conclusion: The work separates decoded expressivity from optimized energy and empirical performance, showing initialization masks can beat depth-based fixes, but explicitly does not establish any quantum computational advantage.

title: Quasi: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation Of Pre-Validated Statements
authors: Dahlia Malkhi Maksym Ioffe
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. Designed for quorum-based systems, QUASI enables parties to attest to external entities that the statement is valid. Surprisingly, each party need not sign the entire statement: authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for the quorum to attest to the whole. A simple deterministic construction illustrates this possibility. Built purely from hashing and error correction, QUASI achieves small per-party contributions and low attestation generation and verification costs, without relying on SNARKs for aggregation. Our main contribution is a randomized construction achieving reductions of more than [MATH] in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures. QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.
tldr: QUASI introduces quorum-based attestation protocols in which each party authenticates only a small subset of symbols of a pre-validated statement, relying solely on hashing and error correction rather than SNARKs.
motivation: Quorum systems need efficient, publicly verifiable attestations of statements without requiring every party to sign the full statement or resort to expensive succinct-proof aggregation.
method: A deterministic construction built from hash functions and error-correcting codes is presented, followed by a randomized construction that shrinks per-party contribution size and hash computation counts.
result: The randomized construction achieves large reductions (orders of magnitude) in per-party contribution size and in hashing costs for attestation generation and verification compared with full hash-based signatures.
conclusion: QUASI is a generic primitive applicable to signature-free consensus attestation and as preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, though it is a classical cryptographic protocol with no quantum-information content.

title: New Classes Of CCZ-Inequivalent Apn Functions With Boomerang Uniformity One In Odd Characteristic: Differential And Boomerang Spectra
authors: Soonhak Kwon Namhun Koo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be an odd prime power and let [MATH] be an even perfect nonlinear (PN) function with [MATH]. We construct almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions [MATH], where [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] is an [MATH]-linearized permutation polynomial. These one-point modifications of [MATH] have boomerang uniformity one, the smallest possible value for APN functions in odd characteristic. We give complete differential and boomerang spectrum formulas and obtain closed-form evaluations for selected constructions based on Coulter--Matthews monomials and Dembowski--Ostrom polynomials. For [MATH], comparison of differential spectra establishes CCZ-inequivalence to all APN monomial families listed in the paper and every APN binomial in the original Ness--Helleseth family or its extension by Zeng et al. We characterize CCZ-equivalence within our construction, showing that any two linearly inequivalent even PN functions over the same field yield CCZ-inequivalent APN functions. We obtain three pairwise CCZ-inequivalent APN functions with boomerang uniformity one over [MATH] for every [MATH], six over [MATH] for every [MATH], and unbounded numbers of such classes in characteristic three. We further prove that CCZ-equivalence and EA-equivalence coincide for functions at Hamming distance at most [MATH] from a PN function, provided that [MATH]. We also show that all our APN functions have the maximal possible algebraic degree [MATH]. Finally, we exhibit both CCZ-equivalent and CCZ-inequivalent APN pairs with boomerang uniformity one at Hamming distance one.
tldr: The paper constructs new families of APN (almost perfect nonlinear) functions in odd characteristic with boomerang uniformity one via one-point modifications of perfect nonlinear functions, and analyzes their differential/boomerang spectra and CCZ-inequivalence classes.
motivation: APN functions with low boomerang uniformity are desirable for cryptographic S-boxes resisting differential and boomerang attacks; the authors aim to expand the known classes of such functions in odd characteristic and clarify their equivalence relations.
method: Starting from an even perfect nonlinear function and an F_q-linearized permutation polynomial, they build one-point modifications, derive closed-form differential and boomerang spectrum formulas for Coulter-Matthews and Dembowski-Ostrom based constructions, and use spectral comparisons to establish CCZ-inequivalence.
result: They obtain complete spectrum formulas, prove maximal algebraic degree, show CCZ-equivalence coincides with EA-equivalence near PN functions under a degree condition, and exhibit three, six, or unbounded numbers of pairwise CCZ-inequivalent APN functions with boomerang uniformity one over various fields.
conclusion: The work substantially enlarges the inventory of CCZ-inequivalent APN functions with optimal boomerang uniformity in odd characteristic, providing a tool for designing cryptographic functions.

title: Wideband Ar-hcf Transmission Under Variable Network Traffic: A System-Level Analysis
authors: Zhiping Jiang Md Ghulam Saber
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic traffic changes spectral occupancy in wideband optical links, perturbing surviving channels in single-mode fiber (SMF) through nonlinear interference (NLI), inter-channel stimulated Raman scattering, and amplifier loading. This motivates amplified-spontaneous-emission (ASE) idlers to maintain full occupancy. We test whether spectral filling remains necessary in antiresonant hollow-core fiber (AR-HCF) using a span-by-span model of a 96-channel, 9.6-THz extended-C+L link over 960 km. The model jointly tracks signal, ASE, and NLI, including amplifier pigtails, line-resolved CO2 absorption, intermodal interference, amplifier control, and load transients. At equal launch power, reducing occupancy from 100% to 20% changes surviving-channel generalized signal-to-noise ratio (GSNR) by just 0.0016 dB in AR-HCF versus 1.52 dB in SMF. At the AR-HCF throughput-optimal launch of +12.3 dBm/channel, the GSNR shift rises to 0.24 dB, nearly all from NLI in short solid-glass amplifier pigtails, chiefly the output pigtail. These pigtails hold the optimum 8.9 dB below the amplifier ceiling, but removing them yields only about 1% more throughput at that launch due to transceiver, intermodal-interference, and gas-absorption limits. Line-resolved gas modeling distinguishes several decibels of CO2 attenuation, largely offset by per-span equalization, from narrow absorption notches not recoverable by flat gain. Constant-gain control permits a 23% amplifier energy saving by tracking load, whereas constant-output control saves none. An 85% channel drop causes an 8.8-dB uncontrolled gain excursion, reduced to 0.6 dB with an assumed 500-Hz loop. Thus, AR-HCF shifts the constraints on elastic wideband transmission from fiber nonlinearities to amplifier-site components, gas absorption, and control dynamics.
tldr: A system-level simulation showing that antiresonant hollow-core fiber (AR-HCF) largely removes fiber-nonlinearity penalties from dynamic spectral occupancy changes in wideband 96-channel C+L transmission, shifting bottlenecks to amplifier-site components, gas absorption, and gain-control dynamics.
motivation: In single-mode fiber, varying traffic load changes spectral occupancy and perturbs surviving channels via nonlinear interference, inter-channel stimulated Raman scattering, and amplifier loading, motivating ASE idlers; the authors ask whether such spectral filling is still needed in AR-HCF.
method: A span-by-span numerical model of a 960 km, 96-channel, 9.6-THz extended-C+L link jointly tracking signal, ASE, and NLI, including amplifier pigtails, line-resolved CO2 absorption, intermodal interference, amplifier control loops, and load transients.
result: At equal launch power, dropping occupancy from 100% to 20% shifts surviving-channel GSNR by only 0.0016 dB in AR-HCF versus 1.52 dB in SMF; at the +12.3 dBm/channel optimum the shift grows to 0.24 dB, dominated by NLI in solid-glass amplifier pigtails, and constant-gain control enables a 23% amplifier energy saving.
conclusion: AR-HCF shifts the constraints on elastic wideband transmission away from fiber nonlinearities toward amplifier-site components, gas absorption notches, and control-loop dynamics, with an 85% channel drop causing an 8.8-dB uncontrolled gain excursion reducible to 0.6 dB with a 500-Hz loop.

title: Bayes-Optimal Quantum Computational Sensing Via Convex Spectral Design
authors: Amirhossein Taherpour, Alireza Sadeghi, Georgios B. Giannakis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computational sensing performs task-specific inference directly through coherent sensing dynamics, avoiding an intermediate estimation step. Existing designs, however, typically optimize quantum control parameters through nonconvex programs whose performance can depend strongly on initialization. This contribution formulates binary phase classification directly in terms of the sensor's measurement response. For a fixed query budget, generalized quantum signal processing (GQSP) restricts this response to a bounded trigonometric polynomial, while the Bayes classification error is linear in the response. These properties yield an exact finite-dimensional semidefinite program for the globally Bayes-optimal sensor response. Fej\'er--Riesz factorization and GQSP synthesis then recover a physically realizable control sequence. The same formulation extends naturally to sample-based design and additive phase uncertainty. Numerical tests show improved accuracy and optimization reliability over direct control-angle training; noise-aware redesign also lowers error under phase uncertainty.
tldr: The paper formulates Bayes-optimal binary phase classification for quantum computational sensing as a convex spectral design problem and synthesizes a physically realizable GQSP control sequence.
motivation: Quantum computational sensing can perform task-specific inference directly from coherent sensing dynamics, but existing control-parameter optimization is nonconvex and initialization-sensitive.
method: The measurement response is restricted by generalized quantum signal processing to a bounded trigonometric polynomial, making the Bayes error linear in the response and enabling an exact finite-dimensional semidefinite program; Fejer-Riesz factorization and GQSP synthesis recover the control sequence.
result: Numerical tests show improved accuracy and optimization reliability over direct control-angle training, and noise-aware redesign reduces error under additive phase uncertainty.
conclusion: The approach provides a convex optimization framework for globally Bayes-optimal quantum sensor responses, but it is specialized to quantum sensing/control and falls outside the researcher's listed core directions.

title: Dynamics Of Squeezed-state Preparation In Quadratic And Kerr Nonlinear Microresonators
authors: S. D. Chikalkin, V. L. Gorshenin, V. E. Lobanov, I. A. Bilenko, D. A. Chermoshentsev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a dynamical model of squeezed-state generation in nonlinear optical microresonators that takes into account the back-action of the signal mode on the pump mode. The resonator is treated as an open quantum system, while the pump modes are described by time-dependent classical amplitudes, which allows pump depletion to be included beyond the standard undepleted-pump approximation. For a [MATH] microresonator, the model reproduces the conventional 3~dB intracavity squeezing limit below threshold and predicts a transient above-threshold regime in which this limit can be overcome for a finite time before pump depletion becomes appreciable. The dynamical approach is extended to a three-mode Kerr microresonator with two pump modes. Separately, we investigate stationary squeezing in a reduced five-mode model with fixed pump amplitudes, including a parasitic single-pump spontaneous four-wave-mixing channel. Within this model, the parasitic channel reduces the achievable squeezing and shifts the instability threshold to lower pump amplitudes. These results provide a compact framework for estimating the validity range of the undepleted-pump approximation and for analyzing transient squeezing dynamics in nonlinear microresonators.
tldr: The paper develops a dynamical model of squeezed-state generation in nonlinear optical microresonators, including pump depletion and Kerr effects.
motivation: Standard squeezed-state models often rely on the undepleted-pump approximation, which may fail when signal back-action and parasitic nonlinear channels are significant.
method: The authors treat the resonator as an open quantum system with classical time-dependent pump amplitudes, extending the analysis to three-mode Kerr and reduced five-mode models.
result: The model reproduces the 3 dB intracavity squeezing limit below threshold and predicts transient above-threshold squeezing beyond this limit before pump depletion dominates; parasitic four-wave mixing reduces squeezing and shifts the instability threshold.
conclusion: The framework provides a compact way to assess the validity of the undepleted-pump approximation and to analyze transient squeezing dynamics in nonlinear microresonators.

title: 2d Polaritons For Squeezing And Shrinking Light
authors: Eduardo Bede Barros, Niclas Sven M\"uller, Stephanie Reich, Christian Thomsen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) materials have emerged as an extraordinary platform for polaritonics, given their remarkable ability to confine light to deep sub-wavelength scales. However, as material thicknesses reach the nanometer limit, macroscopic electrodynamic models become inadequate for the description of light-matter coupling in 2D materials, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of 2D polaritons. In this work, we develop a comprehensive quantum microscopic framework that describes 2D polaritons through a general, scale-less Hamiltonian. Starting from the quantum properties of a polarizable 2D surface, we derive collective excitations and we identify both transverse electric magnetic modes existing outside the light cone. Our results demonstrate that these 2D systems facilitate a powerful synergy between extreme wavelength shrinking and intrinsic quantum squeezing of electric field quadratures. By establishing this theoretical roadmap, our work provides the essential architecture for controlling non-classical states of light at the nanoscale, opening new avenues for high-precision quantum sensing and the development of next-generation optoelectronic devices.
tldr: The paper develops a quantum microscopic framework for 2D polaritons and shows that they can simultaneously confine light to deep subwavelength scales and generate intrinsic squeezing of electric-field quadratures.
motivation: As 2D materials approach nanometer thickness, macroscopic electrodynamic models fail to describe light-matter coupling, leaving a gap in understanding 2D polaritons and their quantum optical properties.
method: The authors construct a scale-less quantum Hamiltonian for a polarizable 2D surface, derive collective excitations, and identify transverse electric and magnetic modes outside the light cone.
result: They find that 2D polaritons combine extreme wavelength shrinking with intrinsic quantum squeezing of electric-field quadratures.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical roadmap for controlling nonclassical light at the nanoscale, with potential applications in quantum sensing and optoelectronic devices.

title: Qaoa Inside Admm: Subproblem Wins Do Not Become Decomposition Wins At Matched Budgets
authors: Sanim Yousuf Fahim Mohammad Arif Hossain
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We benchmark the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) as the binary subproblem solver in a two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for mixed-binary problems against classical solvers under matched budgets. With 23 optimizer evaluations per subproblem, scoring determines the comparison: on its final readout, the optimized QAOA loses to random search at [MATH] and 16 binary variables (inconclusive at 20; exploratory and post hoc tests). When credited with its best sample, it wins. In a noiseless 12-qubit simulation, transferred-angle depth-2 QAOA finds the exact optimum of 97.3\% of planted-family subproblems, against 50.6\%--67.4\% for the four strongest local heuristics (100\% against 90.4\%--94.4\% crediting the four best bitstrings) and a not significantly different 96.5\% for semidefinite rounding with local search (SDP+LS). Under our evaluation-counting convention, its time to solution there is a factor of three to five below the local heuristics' but grows with a larger exponent; it is ten times that of SDP+LS and, in seconds, 54 times that of tabu search with restarts. For the benchmark class, an unconstrained binary quadratic problem in disguise, ADMM's binary step is a proximal step on the reduced problem: at unit penalty ADMM re-solves it, and for larger penalties exact solutions increasingly stall. On two families that do not reduce to one, less accurate solvers found the problem optimum more often at unit and larger penalties. No family gave QAOA a better ADMM outcome than the best classical solver and penalty. The benchmark includes a correctness gate and a log of its hypothesis tests.
tldr: A matched-budget benchmark shows that QAOA's advantage on individual ADMM subproblems does not translate into better end-to-end decomposition performance than classical solvers.
motivation: QAOA is often proposed as a subproblem solver inside classical decomposition frameworks such as ADMM, but it is unclear whether per-subproblem wins survive fair evaluation-count comparisons and yield genuine overall gains.
method: Two-block ADMM for mixed-binary problems is benchmarked with QAOA as the binary subproblem solver (noiseless 12-qubit simulation, transferred-angle depth-2 QAOA, 23 optimizer evaluations per subproblem) against random search, local heuristics, tabu search, and SDP with local search, using a strict evaluation-counting convention plus a correctness gate and logged hypothesis tests.
result: QAOA attains the exact optimum on 97.3% of planted-family subproblems versus 50.6-67.4% for the strongest local heuristics, but is 54x slower than tabu search in seconds and loses to random search under matched budgets at 16 binary variables on final readout; no family gave QAOA a better ADMM outcome than the best classical solver and penalty.
conclusion: Subproblem-level accuracy gains of QAOA do not convert into decomposition-level wins at matched budgets, and for the benchmark class ADMM's binary step is effectively a proximal step that classical solvers handle more efficiently.

title: Realizing Unstructured Pde Forecasting On Superconducting Quantum Processors
authors: Erik Connerty, Jonathan Eastridge, Taylor Patti, Gerasimos Angelatos, Ethan N. Evans
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating high dimensional unstructured Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with quantum processors is a major challenge with significant potential benefit. Existing methods have been demonstrated at small qubit counts, on simplifications of realistic problems. We implement a quantum reservoir network (QRN) for forecasting high-dimensional unstructured PDEs using up to 52 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware. Our method is gradient-free and does not suffer from the challenges of variational quantum algorithms. Instead, the QRN provides a large kernel space, up to 2^52 dimensions and beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, that remains useful under current hardware noise levels. Furthermore, a partial measure-and-reset mechanism enables total circuit runtime for ~24 times the qubit coherence time, so qubit lifetimes do not limit the forecast horizon. Thus, our method enables forecasting realistic unstructured nonlinear PDEs on quantum hardware. Typical difficulties associated with predicting large scale PDEs, such as transpilation, exponential shot requirements, hardware noise, and short qubit lifetimes are mitigated through careful design considerations and a dynamic observable reconstruction method. We validate our approach using a ~34k cell unstructured 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and a challenging nonlinear Gray--Scott reaction--diffusion problem, demonstrating high fidelity prediction on CUDA-Q simulation and on 26 and 52-qubit superconducting quantum processors. Specifically, we show that adding QRN features to an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline reduces prediction error by 21%-43%. Finally, we demonstrate closed-loop autoregressive PDE forecasting on these problems. This work demonstrates, for the first time, quantum circuits with depth beyond qubit lifetimes achieving accurate unstructured mesh forecasting on highly nonlinear PDEs.
tldr: The paper implements a gradient-free quantum reservoir network on up to 52 superconducting qubits to forecast high-dimensional unstructured nonlinear PDEs, demonstrating accurate autoregressive forecasting beyond qubit coherence times via a measure-and-reset mechanism.
motivation: Simulating and forecasting high-dimensional unstructured PDEs is classically challenging, and existing quantum PDE methods are limited to small qubit counts and simplified problems.
method: A quantum reservoir network is used as a large-dimensional feature map, with dynamic observable reconstruction and partial measure-and-reset to extend circuit runtime beyond coherence time; validated on a 34k-cell unstructured cylinder flow and Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion problem.
result: The QRN reduces prediction error by 21%-43% when added to an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline, and closed-loop autoregressive forecasting is demonstrated on 26- and 52-qubit IBM superconducting processors and CUDA-Q simulations.
conclusion: Quantum reservoir computing on current superconducting hardware can forecast realistic unstructured nonlinear PDEs, with circuit depths exceeding qubit lifetimes, but the work is an application of quantum hardware rather than a contribution to the researcher's specified theory-focused directions.

title: Delta-Corrected Shot Reduction For Bypassing Optimization Plateaus In Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
authors: Jamie Evander Ghozaly, Pekik Nurwantoro, Gagus Ketut Sunnardianto, Yanoar P. Sarwono, Leong-Chuan Kwek
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) remains a cornerstone hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for quantum simulation, yet its scalability is fundamentally constrained by heavy measurement overheads. While strategies such as variance-preserved shot reduction (VPSR) mitigates this cost, they suffer from convergence instability and optimization stagnation caused by finite-sample bias in limited pilot shots. To overcome this limitation, we introduce delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR), an analytically enhanced shot allocation strategy that rigorously mitigates finite-sample instability. Utilizing the multivariate delta method, we derive explicit higher-order bias correction terms for the empirical reduction factor. Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations reveal that incorporating higher-order statistical moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, provides the gradient resolution necessary to bypass noise-induced barren plateaus. DSCR significantly accelerates convergence compared to standard VPSR across diverse noise and resource regimes while matching or decreasing cumulative measurement costs, establishing a mathematically rigorous framework for variance-stabilized shot allocation on near-term hardware.
tldr: The paper introduces delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR), a statistical bias-correction strategy for shot allocation in variational quantum eigensolvers to improve convergence and reduce measurement overhead.
motivation: VQE scalability is limited by measurement overhead, and existing variance-preserved shot reduction methods suffer from finite-sample bias, convergence instability, and optimization stagnation.
method: Using the multivariate delta method, the authors derive higher-order bias-correction terms for the empirical reduction factor and incorporate skewness and kurtosis into shot allocation.
result: Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations show that DCSR accelerates convergence relative to standard VPSR across noise and resource regimes while matching or lowering cumulative measurement costs.
conclusion: DCSR provides a mathematically rigorous variance-stabilized shot-allocation framework for near-term VQE hardware, helping bypass noise-induced barren plateaus.

title: Compact Quantum Channel Attention For Static Asl Recognition: A Controlled Study With Parameter-Matched Baselines
authors: Ronak Bhalgami, Deep Kothadiya, Nikita Bhatt
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical models often report good accuracy on image tasks, but it is rarely clear whether the quantum part is responsible. This paper proposes QCA-DenseNet, a static American Sign Language (ASL) recognition pipeline in which an eight-qubit variational circuit acts as a channel-attention gate on DenseNet121 features. The quantum channel attention (QCA) gate has 17,464 parameters, 7.51 times fewer than a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block. The pipeline is tested on 1,815 MU HandImages images by holding out one of five signers at a time, and a frozen-backbone ablation uses small parts of the Kaggle ASL Alphabet data. On unseen signers, QCA-DenseNet reaches 94.50% mean accuracy, above SE (93.72%) and within 0.28 points of the best model. A matched classical MLP and a model without attention perform about the same, and no difference is significant. QCA gives a much smaller attention gate without a detectable loss in accuracy, but no quantum advantage.
tldr: QCA-DenseNet replaces a squeeze-and-excitation attention block with an eight-qubit variational circuit acting as channel attention on DenseNet121 features for static American Sign Language recognition, evaluated against parameter-matched classical baselines.
motivation: Hybrid quantum-classical image models often report strong accuracy, but it is usually unclear whether the quantum component is actually responsible for the gain; this work sets out to test that question in a controlled setting.
method: An eight-qubit variational circuit (17,464 parameters, ~7.5x smaller than an SE block) gates DenseNet121 feature channels, trained on 1,815 MU HandImages images with leave-one-signer-out cross-validation plus a frozen-backbone ablation on a subset of Kaggle ASL Alphabet data.
result: On unseen signers the model reaches 94.50% mean accuracy versus 93.72% for SE and within 0.28 points of the best model, but a matched classical MLP and a no-attention variant perform statistically indistinguishably, with no significant differences.
conclusion: A quantum channel-attention gate achieves comparable accuracy with a much smaller parameter budget, but the study finds no evidence of a quantum advantage.

title: Trained, Frozen, Or Absent: Identifying What A Quantum Layer Contributes To Cross-Sectional Equity Ranking
authors: Chi-Sheng Chen, Xinyu Zhang, En-Jui Kuo, Rong Fu, Qiuzhe Xie, Fan Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid quantumclassical models are increasingly proposed for nancial prediction, but reported gains are rarely separated from the classical components around them. We study a hybrid quantum temporal convolutional network for daily cross-sectional ranking of 2000 Tokyo Stock Exchange equities under a protocol built to make the quantum contribution identiable: six conditions (circuit trained, frozen or absent, a parameter-matched classical surrogate, and the circuit alone, trained or frozen) through one code path; four walk-forward folds with ve seeds; bootstrap intervals, Deated Sharpe Ratios, backtest-overtting probabilities and family-wise error control; ve classical baselines including a gradient-boosted tree; and a locked holdout. On 500 out-of-sample days two one-sided tests place the trained-versus-frozen dierence inside 0.03 annualised Sharpe (p = 0.0055, minimum detectable eect 0.02): the circuit is equivalent to a frozen one, not merely indistinguishable from it. With the circuit as the head's only input the two are equivalent inside 0.25; against the network with no circuit the design resolves only 0.50. No condition is distinguishable from zero (best De-ated Sharpe Ratio 0.17). The holdout reproduces the ablation on a protable window, and 2000 US equities reproduce it where every condition loses money.
tldr: A rigorous ablation study showing that the trained quantum circuit layer in a hybrid quantum-classical model contributes no measurable advantage over a frozen or absent circuit for cross-sectional equity ranking.
motivation: Hybrid quantum-classical models are increasingly claimed to improve financial forecasting, but reported gains are rarely isolated from the classical components surrounding the quantum layer, making the quantum contribution unidentifiable.
method: The authors build a hybrid quantum temporal convolutional network and evaluate six conditions (trained/frozen/absent circuit, parameter-matched classical surrogate, circuit-only variants) through a single code path, using four walk-forward folds with five seeds, bootstrap intervals, Deflated Sharpe Ratios, backtest-overfitting probabilities, family-wise error control, five classical baselines, and a locked holdout on 2000 Tokyo Stock Exchange equities (replicated on 2000 US equities).
result: Two one-sided tests place the trained-versus-frozen difference within 0.03 annualised Sharpe (p = 0.0055, minimum detectable effect 0.02), establishing equivalence; no condition is distinguishable from zero (best Deflated Sharpe Ratio 0.17), and the US replication shows losses for all conditions.
conclusion: The trained quantum layer provides no demonstrable benefit for financial ranking tasks; the paper argues for stricter identifiability protocols when claiming quantum advantage in applied ML.

title: How Light Interacts With Matter, Revisited
authors: Giancarlo Reali
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 1968 Victor Weisskopf explained in Scientific American how light interacts with matter, with a few formulas and many words. We tell the same story again with the tools that have since become available: the fields are computed and drawn, and their evolution in time is shown in animations. Light is described as a classical electromagnetic field and matter as a collection of charged oscillators; every phenomenon follows from adding up the retarded waves radiated by the oscillators, each with its proper delay and phase. From this single picture we obtain the blue of the sky and the white of the clouds, transparency and the refractive index, the Ewald-Oseen extinction theorem, reflection and the colours of thin films, why metals reflect and what gives metals and semiconductors their colours, polarizers, Brewster's angle and birefringence, the working of mirrors, lenses, microscopes and the eye, the propagation of a few-cycle pulse through a slab, Cherenkov radiation, amplification and second-harmonic generation. Feynman's arrows are made quantitative with the sheet method, and coupled-dipole simulations show the incident wave being cancelled and replaced inside the medium. The connection with quantum theory is discussed where the classical picture stops: the photon, spontaneous emission and the forbidden lines of the aurora, vision and photosynthesis, and the sum over paths. The text is addressed to undergraduate students and their teachers, and to any reader curious about the physics behind everyday optical phenomena; derivations are collected in separate panels, and the animations and the Python codes used for the figures and simulations are provided as ancillary files.
tldr: A pedagogical, animation-rich retelling of Weisskopf's 1968 Scientific American account of light-matter interaction using classical charged oscillators and retarded waves.
motivation: The author aims to make the classical oscillator picture of optics intuitive for undergraduate students and teachers by exploiting modern computational and visualization tools that were unavailable in 1968.
method: Light is treated as a classical electromagnetic field and matter as a collection of driven charged oscillators; all phenomena are derived by summing retarded radiated waves with proper delays and phases, supported by coupled-dipole simulations, Python code, and animations.
result: The single framework reproduces a broad catalogue of optical effects — sky blue, cloud white, refractive index and the Ewald-Oseen extinction theorem, thin-film colours, metallic reflection, Brewster angle, birefringence, imaging, few-cycle pulse propagation, Cherenkov radiation, and second-harmonic generation — with brief remarks on where the classical picture gives way to quantum theory.
conclusion: The work is an educational resource rather than a research contribution, offering no new information-theoretic or thermodynamic results relevant to quantum information science.

title: Dispersion Interaction Between Two Bodies Of Arbitrary Shape
authors: Michael V. Davidovich
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Based on the vacuum tensor Green's functions of electrodynamics, the Lippmann-Schwinger-type equations were derived for the correlations of electromagnetic fields. These correlations were applied within the Maxwell stress tensor and the Lorentz force formula to determine Casimir dispersion forces for two arbitrary bodies. The analysis is performed by the excitation of bodies by electric and magnetic dipoles.
tldr: The paper derives Casimir dispersion forces between two arbitrarily shaped bodies using vacuum electromagnetic Green's functions and Lippmann-Schwinger-type correlation equations.
motivation: Casimir/dispersion interactions are important in quantum electrodynamics and nanoscale forces, but accurate calculation for arbitrary geometries remains challenging.
method: The author uses vacuum tensor Green's functions to derive equations for electromagnetic field correlations, then inserts these into the Maxwell stress tensor and Lorentz force formula, considering electric and magnetic dipole excitation.
result: The formalism yields Casimir dispersion forces for two bodies of arbitrary shape via field-correlation equations and stress-tensor evaluation.
conclusion: The work provides a Green's-function-based approach to computing geometry-dependent Casimir forces, but it is not directly connected to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Geometric Stochastic Dynamics And Fokker-Planck Equation On $\mathsf{T}\mathbb S^2$
authors: Adeel Akhtar Hamza Mahmood
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a geometric (coordinate-free) stochastic model of a controlled point mass evolving on the unit two-sphere [MATH], together with the Fokker-Planck equation governing the probability density of the resulting stochastic process. The state manifold is the tangent bundle [MATH]. The Levi-Civita connection of the round metric is used to construct the horizontal-vertical splitting of [MATH] and to convert the intrinsic second-order dynamics of the system into a first-order controlled vector field on [MATH]. Endowing the tangent bundle with the Sasaki metric then permits stochastic perturbations to be introduced intrinsically and independently in horizontal, i.e., position, and vertical, i.e., velocity, directions. The corresponding infinitesimal generator is obtained in horizontal-vertical Hessian form. The probability density is defined with respect to the Sasaki Riemannian volume measure. The Fokker-Planck equation is derived intrinsically in both Stratonovich and It\^o forms. In the It\^o representation, a globally defined horizontal-vertical diffusion tensor yields a compact double-divergence Fokker-Planck PDE. No coordinates or embedded Euclidean representation of the sphere dynamics are used in the development. Numerical simulations illustrate the stochastic motion of a controlled particle ensemble on [MATH] toward an antipodal target configuration.
tldr: The paper constructs a coordinate-free stochastic model of a controlled point mass on the two-sphere using the tangent bundle with Sasaki metric, and derives the corresponding Fokker-Planck equation in both Stratonovich and Itô forms.
motivation: The authors aim to formulate stochastic perturbations of second-order dynamics on a curved manifold intrinsically, avoiding coordinates or embedded Euclidean representations.
method: A horizontal-vertical splitting via the Levi-Civita connection converts the intrinsic second-order dynamics into a first-order controlled vector field on the tangent bundle; the Sasaki metric then allows intrinsic stochastic forcing, yielding the infinitesimal generator and Fokker-Planck equation.
result: The Fokker-Planck equation is obtained in Hessian form and, in the Itô representation, as a compact double-divergence PDE with a globally defined horizontal-vertical diffusion tensor; numerical simulations show an ensemble converging toward an antipodal target.
conclusion: The framework provides a fully geometric treatment of stochastic control on tangent bundles, demonstrated numerically on the sphere.

title: zkARc: Succinctly Verifiable Proofs For Neurosymbolic Natural Language Formalization And Verification
authors: Wyatt Benno (ICME Labs), Alberto Centelles (imperial College London), Aman Goel (amazon Web Services), Benjamin Kiesl-Reiter
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly execute consequential actions on behalf of users, but ordinary middleware guardrails do not provide cryptographic proof that a policy was actually enforced. Their verdicts leave counterparties dependent on the operator unless they repeat the checks themselves, potentially exposing sensitive policies and inputs. We present zkARc, a modular proof-carrying framework that wraps each stage of Automated Reasoning checks (ARc) in an independent, succinctly verifiable zero-knowledge proof. ARc is a neurosymbolic system that translates natural language policies into formal logic and verifies AI-generated content against them using SMT solvers. zkARc certifies the planner's output, the policy's formalization, the action's formalization and both solver queries. The receipt binds these computations to the exact action received and, under the stated assumptions, reveals no additional information about private policies and intermediate model values beyond the declared public information and verdict. This lets a third party check the claimed policy enforcement without re-running the pipeline or trusting the operator. We prove completeness, knowledge soundness and zero knowledge for the composed receipt under explicit assumptions. An implementation on Qwen2-0.5B enforces a spending policy end to end, approving two purchases and denying a third. A full receipt, which also proves model inference, takes about an hour to issue with CPU-only proving and verifies in under a minute, and the solver proof alone is 88 KiB and verifies in 0.3 seconds.
tldr: zkARc is a proof-carrying framework that wraps each stage of a neurosymbolic natural-language policy verification pipeline (ARc) in succinct zero-knowledge proofs so third parties can verify policy enforcement without re-running the pipeline or trusting the operator.
motivation: Autonomous agents act on users' behalf, but ordinary middleware guardrails give no cryptographic guarantee that a policy was actually enforced, forcing counterparties to either trust the operator or re-run checks that expose sensitive policies and inputs.
method: The authors compose independent zk-SNARK-style proofs over the planner's output, the policy formalization, the action formalization, and both SMT solver queries, binding them into a single receipt for the exact action while hiding private inputs; they prove completeness, knowledge soundness, and zero knowledge for the composed receipt under explicit assumptions.
result: An end-to-end implementation on Qwen2-0.5B enforces a spending policy, approving two purchases and denying a third; a full receipt including model inference takes about an hour to generate with CPU-only proving and verifies in under a minute, while the solver proof alone is 88 KiB and verifies in 0.3 s.
conclusion: Zero-knowledge proof composition can make AI policy-enforcement auditable and verifiable by third parties, though proving cost remains high for full inference receipts.

title: Cryptanalysis Of Operad-based Cryptography
authors: Ambrogio Maria Bernardelli
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Commutative operads have been proposed as a platform for public-key cryptography, with protocols for key agreement, key exchange, encryption and authentication, together with a masking technique and families of algebras with secret parameters intended to strengthen them. We show that breaking key agreement, key exchange and encryption reduces to two problems over the centralizer of the public operations: an interpolation problem for key agreement and a division problem for the other two. Neither problem requires recovering a secret, and the set from which secrets are drawn plays no role in these attacks. For the operad platforms in the two original papers (fields, the integers, residue rings, the tropical semiring with finite entries, convexors and the masked tropical algebras), the relevant problems can be solved in polynomial time in the input models specified here, and masking does not affect these attacks. The authentication protocol fails for a more elementary reason: as originally stated it does not bind the prover to any public key, and even with a registered public key the response expected by the verifier can be computed from public data. In the masked variant, verification requires the secret mask; on the concrete string platforms, one observed session with an invertible challenge entry suffices for forgery. We also observe that one of the auxiliary constructions satisfies the algebra axioms only in a degenerate case, although the corresponding protocol remains correct. The attacks are implemented and verified on random instances of representative platforms.
tldr: The paper cryptanalyzes commutative-operad-based public-key cryptography, showing that key agreement, key exchange, encryption, and authentication can be broken via centralizer problems and public-data attacks.
motivation: Commutative operads had been proposed as a platform for public-key cryptographic protocols with masking techniques; this work tests and undermines their security claims.
method: The author reduces breaking key agreement to an interpolation problem over the centralizer of public operations and breaking key exchange/encryption to a division problem, then gives polynomial-time attacks for the specified concrete platforms and verifies them on random instances.
result: The proposed protocols are broken without recovering secrets; masking does not prevent the attacks, and the authentication protocol fails because responses can be computed from public data or forged from one observed session on concrete string platforms.
conclusion: The operad-based cryptographic platforms analyzed are insecure as originally proposed, and the attacks are implemented and verified on representative random instances.

title: PQC-Corpus: A Dataset Of Linked Development Histories For Post-Quantum Cryptography
authors: Souhardya Saha Dip, Moshood A. Fakorede, Umar Farooq
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards evolve, developers must adapt implementations, tests, and protocols. Studying this work requires connecting code changes to problem reports and developer reviews. We present PQC-Corpus, a dataset of linked development histories from 179 public GitHub repositories, spanning cryptographic libraries and general-purpose projects. It connects issues and closing pull requests to commits and full patches, with comments and reviews. We combine Git histories with GitHub threads, reconstruct 23 pull-request commit lists truncated at 250 entries, and check file integrity, schemas, and links. Two annotators independently assessed sampled commits and issues ([MATH] and [MATH]), labeling about seven in ten commits and two in three issues PQC-related within these samples. We provide full and filtered views with removal ledgers, and quantify how filtering reduces links from issues to commits. A patch-free view supports inspection before downloading patches, while traversal scripts follow issues to code changes. We make the dataset and collector publicly available for studies of specification changes, hybrid interoperability, cryptographic review, and migration assistance.
tldr: PQC-Corpus is a public dataset linking GitHub issues, pull requests, commits, and patches across 179 repositories to support empirical studies of post-quantum cryptography migration.
motivation: As PQC standards evolve, developers must adapt implementations and protocols, and studying this work requires connecting code changes to problem reports and reviews — which existing data sources do not conveniently provide.
method: The authors scrape Git histories and GitHub threads from 179 public repositories, reconstruct truncated pull-request commit lists, verify file integrity and link consistency, and have two annotators independently label sampled commits and issues for PQC relevance.
result: Roughly seven in ten sampled commits and two in three sampled issues were labeled PQC-related; the dataset provides full and filtered views with removal ledgers and quantifies how filtering reduces issue-to-commit links.
conclusion: The dataset and collector are released to enable studies of specification changes, hybrid interoperability, cryptographic review, and migration assistance in post-quantum cryptography.

title: A Metric Characterization Of Free Unitary Quantum Groups
authors: Sang-Gyun Youn Yoonje Jeong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a compact matrix quantum group [MATH] with a fundamental unitary representation [MATH] of dimension at least two, the reduced operator norm of the self-adjoint main character satisfies [MATH]. Within the category of free quantum groups of Kac type, it is known that the minimum [MATH] is attained only by free unitary quantum groups. We establish this characterization in full generality, including the non-Kac setting: this minimum is attained if and only if [MATH] is isomorphic to a free unitary quantum group [MATH] as compact matrix quantum groups.
tldr: The paper gives a metric characterization of free unitary quantum groups among compact matrix quantum groups via the reduced operator norm of the main character.
motivation: Previous characterization results within Kac-type free quantum groups are extended to the non-Kac setting, aiming to identify free unitary quantum groups by a minimal operator-norm property.
method: The authors study compact matrix quantum groups and their fundamental unitary representations, analyzing the reduced operator norm of the self-adjoint main character.
result: They prove that the minimum operator norm is attained if and only if the compact matrix quantum group is isomorphic to a free unitary quantum group, including in the non-Kac case.
conclusion: This establishes a full-generality metric characterization of free unitary quantum groups, contributing to the operator-algebraic theory of compact quantum groups rather than to quantum information science.

title: Characterizations Of Minimal Hermitian Completions Via Moments And Subdifferentials
authors: Alejandro Varela Tamara Bottazzi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a Hermitian matrix [MATH] and a real subspace [MATH] of Hermitian matrices, we study the matrices [MATH], [MATH], of minimal spectral norm, which we call [MATH]-minimal. The main motivation is the Hermitian matrix completion problem, where [MATH] is spanned by the Hermitian matrix units corresponding to the unspecified entries. Our main tool is the moment of a subspace [MATH] relative to [MATH], a compact convex subset of [MATH], [MATH], which we relate to the joint numerical range and to the [MATH]-dimensional field of a family of matrices. We compute the subdifferential of [MATH] in terms of the moments of the eigenspaces of the extreme eigenvalues of [MATH], and we obtain several equivalent characterizations of [MATH]-minimality: in terms of eigenvectors, of moments, of subdifferentials and of norm one functionals that annihilate [MATH]. When the identity belongs to [MATH], every [MATH]-minimal matrix has balanced spectrum, and minimality is equivalent to the moments of the eigenspaces of the maximum and minimum eigenvalues having nonempty intersection; we show that this characterization fails if [MATH]. We illustrate the results with several examples, and we prove that the adjacency matrix of a connected graph is minimal for its completion problem if and only if the graph is complete bipartite.
tldr: The paper characterizes minimal-spectral-norm Hermitian matrix completions using moments and subdifferentials of subspaces.
motivation: The work is motivated by the Hermitian matrix completion problem and seeks equivalent characterizations of minimality for matrices constrained by a real subspace of Hermitian matrices.
method: It introduces the moment of a subspace relative to a matrix, relates it to joint numerical range and the field of values, and computes subdifferentials of the spectral norm in terms of eigenspace moments.
result: The authors obtain equivalent characterizations of minimality via eigenvectors, moments, subdifferentials, and norm-one annihilating functionals, and show balanced-spectrum results when the identity lies in the subspace; they also characterize connected graphs whose adjacency matrix is minimal as complete bipartite.
conclusion: The paper provides a convex-analytic and moment-based framework for Hermitian matrix completion, with graph-theoretic applications, but it is a pure matrix-analysis contribution without direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Optimal Sampling And Transmission Policy For Information Freshness In Gossip Networks
authors: Ahmed Arafa Irtiza Hasan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.10952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the optimal sampling and transmission policies for a transmitter communicating with n gossiping receivers with the objective of tracking a source's status over time using a semantic freshness metric: Version Age of Information (VAoI). The transmitter observes the version changes in the source, and can acquire a new information version by paying a sampling cost. The receivers gossip, allowing information exchange among each other without direct transmission. Gossiping can save on transmission cost, but it may propagate stale version information, necessitating transmitter intervention. With imperfect communication links, we formulate an infinite horizon average cost Markov Decision Process (MDP) in order to jointly optimize receivers' VAoIs, sampling and transmission costs in a time slotted fully connected (FC) gossip network. We first solve the MDP using Relative Value Iteration (RVI) algorithm. Then, we prove that the sampling decision has a threshold structure in the transmitter VAoI. Further, under reliable gossiping links, we show that transmission and idling has an VAoI-difference threshold structure with minimum VAoI activation. Numerical results obtained using RVI show that the optimal policy consistently outperforms natural baselines. These results characterize how source sampling, direct transmission, and receiver gossip should be jointly coordinated for cost-aware semantic freshness in gossip networks.
tldr: The paper optimizes sampling and transmission policies for minimizing Version Age of Information in gossip networks using a Markov decision process.
motivation: It aims to coordinate source sampling, direct transmission, and receiver gossip to maintain semantic freshness while accounting for sampling and transmission costs.
method: The authors formulate an infinite-horizon average-cost MDP for a fully connected gossip network with imperfect links and solve it via relative value iteration, proving threshold structures for sampling and transmission decisions.
result: The optimal policy is shown to have threshold properties and consistently outperforms natural baselines in numerical experiments.
conclusion: Jointly coordinating sampling, transmission, and gossip can achieve cost-aware information freshness in classical gossip networks.

title: On The Seven-particle Clusters Of Lennard-Jones And Thomson
authors: Li Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.09925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this Letter, we develop a graph-geometric framework and prove that the pentagonal bipyramid (PBP) is the unique global minimiser of both the seven-particle Lennard-Jones energy in [MATH] and the seven-charge Thomson energy on [MATH], up to rigid symmetries and particle relabelling. For the Thomson problem, this strengthens a recent deterministic global-optimality certificate to numerical tolerance into an exact global-optimality and uniqueness theorem. A weak-interaction graph, defined by thresholding pair geometry, organises configuration space without imposing symmetry or discarding any pair interaction. For Lennard-Jones, pair-energy counting, graph classification, subset bounds, and force balance reduce all possible minimisers to 29 bounded domains; exact geometric certificates exclude 28, localise the survivor near the PBP, and a uniform restoring-energy estimate proves uniqueness. The Thomson proof follows the same progression: graph reduction, geometric localisation, and rigidity, but finalises through whole-domain coercivity and a global localisation theorem. The same fivefold order therefore emerges in two very different physical settings: an unconstrained cluster with a preferred bond length and purely repelling charges confined to a sphere, showing a common geometric organising principle for seven particles that is not tied to either interaction.
tldr: This paper proves that the pentagonal bipyramid is the unique global minimizer for seven-particle Lennard-Jones and Thomson cluster energies using a graph-geometric framework.
